input: Feedback control is explained here by means of a temperature loop on a process vessel, in which the temperature of the vessel is held at a desired value by adjusting the heating applied to it. The starting point of the loop is the sensor, which measures the temperature of the vessel contents and converts the measurement into a signal the controller can use. The measurement is the only information about the vessel that the loop possesses, so if the sensor reads high or low by a fixed amount, every later action of the loop is displaced by the same amount, and what the loop holds is the indicated temperature rather than the true temperature. The signal from the sensor passes to the controller, which compares the measured value with the set point, the value at which the temperature is required to be held. The difference between the measurement and the set point is the error, and on the basis of this error the controller determines its output, changing it in the direction that reduces the error, by an amount governed by the control action configured. The controller output passes to the final element, which in this loop is a control valve in the line supplying the heating medium. Opening the valve allows more heating medium to flow and increases the heat input to the vessel, whereas closing the valve reduces the heat input correspondingly. The feedback in this arrangement is negative in sign: an increase in the measured temperature above the set point leads to a reduction in the heat input, while a decrease leads to an increase, so the loop acts against the deviation that gave rise to the action. It is this sign that makes the arrangement a regulating loop, since if the sign were reversed, an increase in temperature would call for still more heat, and the deviation would grow rather than being corrected.
target: A temperature loop controls the temperature of a process vessel by feedback. The loop holds the vessel temperature at its set point, the value the temperature is required to keep, by adjusting the heating of the vessel in response to the measured temperature. The sensor measures the temperature of the vessel contents and converts the measurement into a signal the controller can use. The measurement is the loop's only knowledge of the vessel: a sensor that reads high or low by a fixed amount displaces every later action of the loop by the same amount, and the loop holds the indicated temperature, not the true one. The controller receives the measurement and compares it with the set point. The difference between the two, the error, sets the controller's output: the controller changes its output in the direction that reduces the error, by an amount its control action determines. The final element receives the controller output and changes the heating of the vessel. In this loop the final element is a control valve in the line that supplies the heating medium: opening the valve admits more heating medium and raises the heat input, and closing the valve reduces the heat input. The feedback is negative. A rise in the measured temperature above the set point reduces the heat input, and a fall in the measured temperature increases it, so the loop acts against the deviation that produced the action. The sign is what makes the loop a regulating loop. With the opposite sign, a rise in temperature would call for more heat, and the deviation would grow instead of being corrected.
